paragraphs.heading: A slow slide in pH
paragraphs.text: Ocean acidification is the continuing drop in the pH of Earth's ocean. Between 1950 and 2026, the average pH at the surface slid from about 8.15 to about 8.05. The numbers look close, but the pH scale is logarithmic, so a 0.1 change means 26% more hydrogen ions. Seawater is still alkaline, with a pH above 8; it is becoming more acidic, not acidic.

paragraphs.heading: The chemistry behind it
paragraphs.text: The main cause is carbon dioxide from human activity, and CO₂ in the air passed 422 ppm in 2024. The ocean takes up roughly a quarter of the CO₂ that people emit. Once absorbed, CO₂ forms carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which breaks apart into a hydrogen ion (H⁺) plus a bicarbonate ion (HCO−3). Those free hydrogen ions are what push the pH down.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same everywhere
paragraphs.text: Surface pH and carbonate levels vary with depth and location. Colder water at higher latitudes can absorb more CO₂, which can push acidity up there. Local conditions matter too: currents and upwelling, nearby large rivers, sea ice cover, and exchange with the air of nitrogen and sulfur released by fossil fuel burning and farming.

paragraphs.heading: Shell builders at risk
paragraphs.text: Animals that build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, such as mollusks and corals, are especially exposed. Extra CO₂ in seawater lowers the saturation of the carbonate minerals they use. Scientists have also seen reduced calcification, weaker immune responses and less energy for basic tasks such as reproduction.

paragraphs.heading: Why people should care
paragraphs.text: These effects reach people too. Around one billion people rely wholly or partly on the fishing, tourism and coastal management services that coral reefs provide. So continued acidification could threaten food chains tied to the ocean.

paragraphs.heading: Past and future
paragraphs.text: Acidification has happened before in Earth's history, and the ecological collapse that followed had lasting effects on the carbon cycle and climate. Today's high CO₂ levels and their fast rise have no match in the geological record of the past 55 million years. Cutting carbon dioxide emissions is one of the only fixes that tackles the root cause, and removing CO₂ from the air would also help reverse it. Ocean-based ideas such as ocean alkalinity enhancement and enhanced weathering are being studied, but they are generally far from ready and carry many risks.
